# Growth faltering

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Pediatrics > Child development and wellbeing > Growth faltering*

[Original Article Link](/library/Wt0Pc3)

---

## Summary

Growth faltering is defined as a pattern of slow <u>growth in children</u> when compared to the predicted values for their age and sex. It is seen in up to 10% of children in the United States and often occurs secondary to <u>malnutrition</u>, which can be due to a complex interplay between biological and psychosocial factors. The primary mechanisms that contribute to growth faltering and <u>malnutrition</u> are inadequate nutritional intake, inadequate absorption, and increased metabolic requirements. Clinical features may include signs of <u>malnutrition</u> such as muscle mass wasting, minimal <u>adiposity</u>, <u>hair</u> loss, <u>developmental delay</u>, and recurrent infections. Growth faltering is confirmed using standardized growth charts (e.g., <u>weight-for-age</u> < 5<sup>th</sup> <u>percentile</u>). Clinicians should perform a holistic approach to history and examination to identify <u>risk factors</u> and the underlying etiology. Diagnostic testing is reserved for children with no response to initial management or severe clinical features and can include <u>urinalysis</u>, stool tests, or specific tests depending on the suspected etiology (e.g., <u>HIV test</u>). Management consists of treatment of the underlying cause and nutritional modifications. Most patients can be successfully managed as outpatients. Close follow-up is indicated to prevent relapses or excessive weight gain.

---

## Definitions

* Growth faltering

* A pattern of slow <u>growth in children</u> compared to the predicted values for their age and sex

* Commonly used criteria include: [[2]](/library/nF17ii0)[[3]](/library/LF1wii0)

* <u>Weight-for-age</u>, length-for-age; , <u>BMI</u>-for-age, or weight-for-length < 5<sup>th</sup> <u>percentile</u> [[2]](/library/nF17ii0)[[3]](/library/LF1wii0)

* A decrease across 2 major <u>percentile</u> lines from an already established <u>growth velocity</u> [[2]](/library/nF17ii0)[[3]](/library/LF1wii0)

* Childhood wasting

* Low body weight as a result of acute <u>malnutrition</u>, rapid weight loss, or insufficient weight gain

* Characterized by a <u>z score</u> below 2 standard deviations in <u>BMI</u>-for-age charts or weight-for-length charts

* Growth stunting

* Reduced height as a result of chronic <u>malnutrition</u>

* Characterized by a <u>z score</u> below 2 <u>standard deviations</u> in height-for-age charts; weight may be proportional for height

## Epidemiology

* Seen in up to 10% of children in the United States [[2]](/library/nF17ii0)

* Most commonly occurs in children aged 6–18 months of age [[4]](/library/9dWNH40)




Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Etiology

Growth faltering occurs secondary to <u>malnutrition</u>, often due to a complex interplay between biological and psychosocial factors. [[2]](/library/nF17ii0)[[3]](/library/LF1wii0)[[5]](/library/qF1CQi0)




### <u>Risk factors</u> [[2]](/library/nF17ii0)[[3]](/library/LF1wii0)




* Biological [[3]](/library/LF1wii0)

* <u>Prematurity</u> and <u>low birth weight</u>

* <u>Intrauterine growth restriction</u> [[2]](/library/nF17ii0)

* Congenital anomalies

* <u>Developmental delay</u>

* <u>Autism spectrum disorder</u> [[2]](/library/nF17ii0)

* <u>Gastroesophageal reflux</u>

* <u>Dental caries</u>

* Psychosocial (see also “<u>Social determinants of health</u>”) [[3]](/library/LF1wii0)[[5]](/library/qF1CQi0)

* Low <u>socioeconomic status</u>  [[2]](/library/nF17ii0)

* In the caregiver: <u>stress</u>, social isolation, <u>inexperience</u>, or untreated mental illness [[2]](/library/nF17ii0)[[3]](/library/LF1wii0)[[5]](/library/qF1CQi0)

* Restrictive diets  [[6]](/library/DdW1H40)





> [!TIP]
> Growth faltering is more common in children with multiple <u>risk factors</u>. [[3]](/library/LF1wii0)




### Mechanisms




| <br>Overview of mechanisms of growth faltering [[2]](/library/nF17ii0)[[3]](/library/LF1wii0)<br> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mechanism |  | Common causes |
| Insufficient calorie consumption | <br>Poor oral intake (most common) [[3]](/library/LF1wii0)<br> | <br><br>* <u>Breastfeeding</u> difficulties (e.g., inadequate supply, ineffective latching)<br><br>* Incorrect preparation of formula feeds<br><br>* Poor feeding practices<br><br>* Mechanical difficulties (e.g., <u>cleft palate</u> and/or lip)<br><br>* Poor oral neuromotor coordination<br><br>* <u>Child maltreatment</u><br><br>* Psychiatric disorders (<u>avoidant restrictive food intake disorder</u>, <u>anorexia nervosa</u>)<br><br>* Conditions affecting appetite, e.g., <u>pain</u> from <u>GERD</u>, <u>anorexia</u> secondary to <u>lead poisoning</u><br><br><br> |
| <br>Increased requirements [[2]](/library/nF17ii0)[[3]](/library/LF1wii0)<br> | <br><br>* Inflammatory: inflammatory bowel disease, <u>asthma</u><br><br>* <u>Malignancy</u><br><br>* <u>Congenital heart defects</u><br><br>* <u>Chronic lung disease of prematurity</u><br><br>* Renal impairment<br><br>* Chronic and/or recurrent infections (e.g., <u>HIV</u>, <u>tuberculosis</u>)<br><br><br> |  |
| <br>Inadequate absorption [[2]](/library/nF17ii0)[[3]](/library/LF1wii0)<br> |  | <br><br>* Gastrointestinal disease, e.g., <u>celiac disease</u>, <u>inflammatory bowel disease</u>, infections (e.g., <u>Giardia lamblia</u>)<br><br>* <u>Food intolerance</u> (e.g., milk protein <u>allergy</u>)<br><br>* <u>Cystic fibrosis</u>  [[7]](/library/vdWA740)<br><br>* <u>Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis</u> [[2]](/library/nF17ii0)<br><br>* <u>Iron-deficiency anemia</u><br><br>* <u>Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency</u><br><br>* <u>Cholestasis</u> including <u>biliary atresia</u><br><br><br> |
| <br>Defective energy utilization [[2]](/library/nF17ii0)<br> |  | <br><br>* <u>Inborn errors of metabolism</u>, e.g., <u>glycogen storage disease</u><br><br>* <u>Trisomy 21</u><br><br>* <u>Trisomy 18</u><br><br><br> |

---

## Clinical features

Growth faltering is a manifestation of <u>malnutrition</u> and may be accompanied by features of other underlying conditions. [[2]](/library/nF17ii0)[[3]](/library/LF1wii0)




### Features of <u>malnutrition</u> [[2]](/library/nF17ii0)




* Failure to gain weight

* <u>Clinical features of acute malnutrition in children</u>, e.g.,

* Wasted muscle mass

* Minimal <u>adiposity</u>

* <u>Growth stunting</u>

* Dermatologic signs

* Thin, weak <u>hair</u>

* Pale, dry <u>skin</u>

* Features of <u>micronutrient</u> deficiencies, such as: [[8]](/library/Az1Rvj0)

* <u>Acral dermatitis</u> or change to <u>hair</u> color/texture in <u>zinc deficiency</u>

* <u>Pallor</u> in <u>iron deficiency anemia</u>

* <u>Developmental delay</u>

* Recurrent infections





> [!TIP]
> Persistent severe <u>malnutrition</u> affects growth parameters sequentially; the first affected is weight, then length, and finally head circumference. [[3]](/library/LF1wii0)




### Features of underlying conditions [[3]](/library/LF1wii0)




Features depend on the cause, examples include:




* Suspicious <u>contusions</u> or <u>fractures</u>; abnormal language, social, or psychological development in children who experience abuse

* Recurrent <u>vomiting</u> and <u>diarrhea</u> in gastrointestinal diseases

* <u>Atopic dermatitis</u> in <u>food allergies</u>

* <u>Heart murmur</u> in <u>congenital cardiac disease</u>

* Dysmorphic features in genetic abnormalities

* <u>Edema</u> in renal or <u>liver</u> failure

---

## Diagnosis

### Approach [[2]](/library/nF17ii0)[[3]](/library/LF1wii0)




* Obtain growth measurements and plot them on growth charts appropriate to age and any underlying conditions.  [[2]](/library/nF17ii0)[[3]](/library/LF1wii0)

* Confirm growth faltering by identifying either:

* Single point measurements in low <u>percentiles</u>

* OR significant delays in linear growth

* Perform a comprehensive clinical assessment to identify the <u>etiology of growth faltering</u>.

* Consider diagnostic studies in patients with: [[2]](/library/nF17ii0)[[3]](/library/LF1wii0)

* Suspected <u>micronutrient</u> deficiencies

* Severe clinical features (e.g., weight gain <u>velocity</u> < 25% of expected)

* No response to initial management

* Concurrently assess for <u>abnormal pediatric development</u>.  [[3]](/library/LF1wii0)





> [!TIP]
> Diagnostics studies are not required unless there are concerning features in the history or <u>physical examination</u>. [[2]](/library/nF17ii0)




### Clinical assessment [[2]](/library/nF17ii0)[[3]](/library/LF1wii0)




* Comprehensive <u>pediatric history and physical examination</u> including <u>family history</u> and prenatal/<u>birth</u> history

* Feeding and nutrition history

* Number and frequency of feeds

* Food refusal

* Observation of a feed  [[9]](/library/TB16Zj0)

* <u>Social history</u>: identify <u>risk factors</u> such as <u>food insecurity</u>, lower <u>socioeconomic status</u>

* Identify features suggestive of an underlying etiology (see “<u>Clinical features of growth faltering</u>”).





> [!TIP]
> Because growth faltering is commonly multifactorial, a thorough clinical assessment is necessary to address the interplay of contributing biological and psychosocial factors. [[5]](/library/qF1CQi0)[[10]](/library/oF10Qi0)




> [!TIP]
> A period of <u>catch-down growth</u> may occur in children born <u>large for gestational age</u>, reflecting a physiological slowing of growth towards normal patterns. [[11]](/library/eaVxjG0)




### Diagnostic studies




#### Common studies [[2]](/library/nF17ii0)[[3]](/library/LF1wii0)




There is no standard set of blood tests to order; common studies include: [[2]](/library/nF17ii0)[[3]](/library/LF1wii0)




* <u>CBC with differential</u> for <u>anemia</u>, <u>immunodeficiency</u>, or <u>malignancy</u> [[2]](/library/nF17ii0)[[3]](/library/LF1wii0)

* <u>CMP</u> for <u>electrolyte</u> disturbances and <u>renal tubular acidosis</u> [[2]](/library/nF17ii0)[[3]](/library/LF1wii0)

* <u>Thyroid function tests</u>: <u>Hypothyroidism</u> can cause <u>short stature</u>. [[2]](/library/nF17ii0)[[3]](/library/LF1wii0)

* <u>Urinalysis</u> for <u>glycosuria</u>, infection, or renal pathology [[2]](/library/nF17ii0)

* <u>Stool microscopy</u> and culture for infection or <u>malabsorption</u> [[2]](/library/nF17ii0)

* <u>Diagnostic studies for celiac disease</u> [[2]](/library/nF17ii0)

* Lead and <u>iron</u> levels





#### Further studies [[2]](/library/nF17ii0)[[3]](/library/LF1wii0)




Consider additional studies guided by clinical suspicion, for example: [[2]](/library/nF17ii0)




* <u>Aspiration</u>: <u>modified barium swallow</u>

* Gastrointestinal conditions 

* <u>Esophagogastroduodenoscopy</u> with <u>biopsies</u>

* <u>Upper gastrointestinal series</u> with <u>small bowel follow-through</u>

* <u>Fecal calprotectin</u>

* <u>Cholestatic jaundice</u> (e.g., <u>biliary atresia</u>): <u>liver chemistries</u> and imaging

* <u>Food allergies</u>: <u>IgE</u> <u>skin prick test</u>

* <u>Congenital heart disease</u>: <u>echocardiogram</u>

* <u>Cystic fibrosis</u>: <u>sweat test</u>, <u>CFTR</u> <u>genetic testing</u>

* Infections: <u>tuberculosis screening</u>

* <u>Immunodeficiency</u>: <u>immunoglobulin</u> levels for <u>congenital immunodeficiency disorders</u>, <u>HIV screening</u>

---

## Management

### Approach




* Determine <u>malnutrition</u> severity and whether inpatient management is required.

* Severe <u>malnutrition</u> or other <u>admission criteria for growth faltering</u>: inpatient management

* Mild or moderate <u>malnutrition</u>: Trial outpatient management.

* Educate parents on behavioral modifications for mealtimes.

* Refer families with <u>food insecurity</u> to social work or community resources.

* Calculate additional calories required for <u>catch-up growth</u> and start <u>nutritional modifications for growth faltering</u>.

* Replete <u>micronutrient</u> deficiencies, if present.

* Treat any underlying etiology and address <u>modifiable risk factors</u>.

* Ensure immunizations are up to date.

* Arrange regular follow-ups to ensure adequate growth.  [[2]](/library/nF17ii0)[[3]](/library/LF1wii0)





> [!TIP]
> <u>Appetite stimulants</u> are not routinely recommended but may be considered in select cases, e.g., children undergoing cancer treatment. [[3]](/library/LF1wii0)




### <u>Malnutrition</u> severity




Ensure children are measured correctly, e.g., by a trained professional using a calibrated scale with <u>infants</u> unclothed and older children in undergarments or lightweight clothing. [[2]](/library/nF17ii0)[[12]](/library/ZVWZG40)




| <br>Classification of <u>malnutrition</u> [[2]](/library/nF17ii0)<br> |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | Mild | Moderate | Severe |
| Single-point assessment (<u>z score</u>) | <br><br>* Weight-for-height/<u>BMI</u>: -1 to -1.9<br><br>* OR <u>mid-upper arm circumference</u>: -1 to -1.9<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Weight-for-height/<u>BMI</u>: -2 to -2.9<br><br>* OR <u>mid-upper arm circumference</u>: -2 to -2.9<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Weight-for-height/<u>BMI</u>: ≤ -3<br><br>* OR length/height: ≤ -3<br><br>* OR <u>mid-upper arm circumference</u>: ≤ -3<br><br><br> |
| Weight gain <u>velocity</u> | <br>* < 75% of expected weight gain<br><br> | <br>* < 50% of expected weight gain<br><br> | <br>* < 25% of expected weight gain<br><br> |
| Weight loss | <br>* 5% usual body weight<br><br> | <br>* 7.5% usual body weight<br><br> | <br>* 10% usual body weight<br><br> |
| Deceleration of<br>weight-for-height or height | <br>* Decline of 1 <u>z-score</u><br><br> | <br>* Decline of 2 <u>z-scores</u><br><br> | <br>* Decline of 3 <u>z-scores</u><br><br> |





> [!TIP]
> Serial measurements allow for dynamic assessment of growth faltering. [[2]](/library/nF17ii0)




### Inpatient management of growth faltering




Inpatient management allows subspecialist workup of underlying causes, structured feeding evaluations, and intensive provision of <u>nutritional support</u> and caregiver education (see “<u>Outpatient management of growth faltering</u>”).




#### Admission criteria for growth faltering




* Severe <u>malnutrition</u> or <u>dehydration</u>

* Serious underlying medical issues

* Extreme psychosocial factors that do not allow for successful outpatient management

* Need for precise and specific documentation of nutrition

* Unsuccessful outpatient management





#### Inpatient management




* Start the <u>10 steps of recovery for severely undernourished children</u>.

* Monitor for <u>refeeding syndrome</u>.

* Involve multidisciplinary teams in the assessment and management of the child.

* See also “Treatment of <u>protein-energy malnutrition</u>.”





### Outpatient management of growth faltering




The majority of children with growth faltering can be managed as outpatients.




#### Caregiver education on feeding [[2]](/library/nF17ii0)[[13]](/library/sF1tji0)




* Provide a balanced diet with a variety of foods to try.

* Avoid snacking (and drinks other than water) between meals.

* Schedule regular mealtimes where everyone eats together.

* Limit mealtimes to 20–30 minutes.

* Allow children to self-feed; avoid force-feeding.

* Provide <u>positive reinforcement</u>.





#### Nutritional modifications for growth faltering [[2]](/library/nF17ii0)




* Determine caloric intake required to reach ideal weight-for-height. [[2]](/library/nF17ii0)[[3]](/library/LF1wii0) 

* The dietary reference intake for young children is:

* 0–6 months of age: 108 Kcal/kg/day

* 6–12 months of age: 98 Kcal/kg/day

* 1–3 years of age: 102 Kcal/kg/day

* Catch-up caloric requirement (in Kcal/kg/day) = dietary reference intake (in Kcal/kg/day) × ideal weight-for-height  [[3]](/library/LF1wii0)

* <u>Infants</u>

* If <u>breastfeeding</u>: Refer to a lactation consultant.

* Increase the volume of <u>breast milk</u> or formula during feeds (as tolerated).

* Consider increasing the caloric density of feeds.

* Children [[2]](/library/nF17ii0)

* Preferred: increasing calorie-dense foods

* Alternative: supplemental high-calorie drinks





### Follow-up [[2]](/library/nF17ii0)[[3]](/library/LF1wii0)




* Schedule regular appointments.

* Weekly appointments may be appropriate initially, moving to monthly or every few months.

* <u>Infants</u> may require more intensive follow-up.

* Weigh children every few days to one week.

* Initially, catch-up growth should occur.

* Rapid growth at up to 2–3 times the normal rate

* Growth should continue until an acceptable weight-for-length or <u>BMI</u>-for-age <u>z score</u> is attained (usually 4–9 months).  [[3]](/library/LF1wii0)

* Monitor children long-term to ensure appropriate weight gain <u>velocity</u>.

* Relapse may occur if underlying etiology is inadequately addressed.

* Excessive weight gain may also occur and should be avoided.





> [!TIP]
> Measure weight every few days on a calibrated scale, at the same time of day with the same clothing on. [[3]](/library/LF1wii0)
